tips.title: Glycogen is the store, glucagon the hormone
tips.body: Two letters apart and constantly swapped. **Glycogen** sits in the liver; **glucagon** comes from the pancreas and releases glucose from it. Say the word out loud before writing it — glucaGON sends glucose **gone** into the blood.

tips.title: Insulin does two things
tips.body: It moves glucose **into cells**, and it makes the **liver and muscles store it as glycogen**. Most answers give only the first. Both are needed for full marks, and they are the two halves of how the level actually comes down.

tips.title: Type 1 makes none, type 2 ignores it
tips.body: **Type 1**: not enough insulin **produced**. **Type 2**: the cells **do not respond** to it. That one line also explains the treatments — injecting insulin fixes a shortage, not a lack of response.

tips.title: Square the height, in metres
tips.body: $\text{BMI} = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{height}^2}$. Show height² on its own line in your working. For an adult, mass ÷ height (not squared) is roughly 1.7 times the correct BMI, which can still look like a real BMI, so a range check will not always catch it.

tips.title: Correlation is not cause
tips.body: A link between BMI and type 2 diabetes is a **correlation**. What makes the case for cause is the **mechanism** — fat makes cells less responsive — and the fact that **losing weight lowers the risk**. Say all three.

why.matters:
Every cell runs on glucose, and both too much and too little are dangerous — so the concentration in the blood has to be held steady while you eat, fast, sleep and sprint.

It is the clearest case of negative feedback in the course because it uses **two** hormones pushing opposite ways, with the liver as the store they both act on. And when the loop breaks, it breaks in two quite different places, which is exactly the difference between the two kinds of diabetes.

examples.title: Why your blood sugar is the same before and after breakfast
examples.body:
A meal puts a large amount of glucose into the blood in a few minutes, and an hour later the concentration is back where it started. Two hormones from the **pancreas** do that, and they work in opposite directions.

Too high and **insulin** is released: the liver takes glucose out of the blood and stores it as **glycogen**. Too low and **glucagon** is released: the liver turns glycogen back into glucose. Same organ, same store, opposite instructions — which is why the level can be pushed back from either side.

examples.title: Two diabetes, two different failures
examples.body:
They share a name and a symptom and almost nothing else. In **type 1** the pancreas stops producing insulin at all, so the signal is never sent — which is why it is treated by **injecting** insulin, and why diet alone cannot fix it.

In **type 2** the insulin is there and the **cells stop responding** to it. Injecting more of a signal that is being ignored is not the first answer, so treatment starts with diet and exercise. Knowing which end of the loop has failed tells you the treatment, which is why the distinction is worth more than the two names.

visual.alt: A table of the two kinds of diabetes: in type 1 the pancreas stops making insulin and it is treated by injection, while in type 2 the cells stop responding to insulin and treatment begins with diet and exercise

examples.title: Why a runner eats before the race and not during it
examples.body:
Glycogen in the liver and the muscles is the body's short-term store, and it is not large. Endurance athletes fill it in the days before an event, because once it is gone the body has to switch to slower fuels and the pace collapses.

That is the same negative feedback loop seen from the other side. Steady blood glucose while running is glucagon quietly releasing the store, and the limit is not willpower but how much glycogen there was to begin with — which is also why a glucose drink is taken during a long race rather than a meal.

visual.alt: A flow chart of blood glucose during exercise: glucose is used up, the level starts to fall, glucagon is released, and as long as there is glycogen left in the liver the level is held steady

steps.title: Why blood glucose must be controlled
steps.body:
Every cell needs **glucose** for **respiration**, so the blood must always carry some. But the concentration has to be held within narrow limits, and both directions are dangerous.

- **Too low** and cells — brain cells especially — cannot respire fast enough to work properly.
- **Too high** and water is drawn **out of cells by osmosis**, damaging them, and glucose begins to appear in the urine.

The level naturally rises after a **meal**, as carbohydrate is digested and glucose is absorbed into the blood, and falls during **exercise**, as muscles respire it. So something must actively push it back each time. The change can come from inside the body, such as digesting a meal, or from outside it, such as a missed meal or a day of hard physical work, and the body responds the same way to both.

That something is the **pancreas**, which produces **two** hormones with opposite effects:

- **Insulin**, when the level is **too high**
- *(Higher tier only.)* **Glucagon**, when the level is **too low**

Having a hormone for each direction is what lets the body correct a change either way — the negative feedback you met with thyroxine, now with two effectors instead of one.

steps.title: Glucagon: bringing the level up
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)* When blood glucose is **too low**, the **pancreas** releases **glucagon**.

Glucagon causes the **liver to convert glycogen back into glucose**, which is released into the blood. The concentration **rises** back to normal.

So the two hormones are mirror images, and the store they work on is the same:

- **Insulin**: glucose → glycogen. The level **falls**.
- **Glucagon**: glycogen → glucose. The level **rises**.

**The two words are dangerously alike**, and swapping them is the commonest error in this topic. A way to keep them apart: **glucaGON** puts glucose back **on** the move — it sends glucose **out** into the blood. Or note that **glycoGEN** is the stored form, so the hormone whose name is furthest from it, **insulin**, is the one that makes it.

Adrenalin, from the previous topic, also raises blood glucose by the same route — the liver converting glycogen into glucose. So three hormones act on the liver's glycogen store, two of them raising the level and one lowering it.

steps.title: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
steps.body:
**Diabetes** is a failure of this control system, and the two types fail in **different places**. Getting that distinction right is most of the marks in this section.

**Type 1 diabetes.** The **pancreas stops producing enough insulin** — often none at all. It usually begins in childhood or early adulthood and is not caused by lifestyle. Without insulin, blood glucose rises dangerously after every meal.

*Control*: **insulin injections**, timed around meals and exercise, together with monitoring the diet and blood glucose level.

**Type 2 diabetes.** The pancreas still makes insulin, but the **body cells stop responding to it** — they become resistant. The result is the same, a blood glucose level that stays too high, but the cause is elsewhere.

*Control*: a **carbohydrate-controlled diet** and **more exercise**, which reduce the glucose entering the blood and the amount stored. Drugs may be used if that is not enough.

The simplest way to hold the difference:

**Type 1: not enough insulin. Type 2: the cells do not respond to it.**

And it explains the treatments. Injecting insulin fixes a shortage, so it works for type 1. It is much less use if the cells are ignoring the insulin already there — which is why type 2 is managed mainly through diet and exercise.

steps.title: BMI and waist to hip ratio
steps.body:
**Obesity is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes**, and two measurements are used to assess body mass. Both appear in calculation questions.

**Body mass index** uses the equation given on the specification:

$$\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{mass (kg)}}{\left(\text{height (m)}\right)^2}$$

The height is **squared**, and it must be in **metres** — a height given in centimetres is a conversion waiting to be missed.

**Waist to hip ratio** is simply the waist measurement divided by the hip measurement. Both must be in the **same unit**, and then the ratio has no unit at all. It matters because fat carried around the **abdomen** is more strongly linked to type 2 diabetes than fat elsewhere, and a higher ratio indicates more of it.

steps.title: Going deeper: correlation is not cause
steps.body:
**What spec point 7.17 is really asking.** It says *evaluate the correlation between body mass and type 2 diabetes*. The word **correlation** is chosen deliberately, and the mark is for knowing what a correlation does and does not establish.

A **correlation** means two things vary together: as BMI rises across a population, so does the rate of type 2 diabetes. That is a real and strong pattern, and it is good evidence.

But a correlation **does not by itself prove cause**. Three other explanations are always possible:

- **The reverse.** Perhaps the condition causes the weight gain rather than the other way round.
- **A third factor.** Diet and level of exercise both affect body mass **and** affect diabetes risk directly, so they could produce the pattern without body mass itself being the cause.
- **Chance**, though a large study makes this unlikely.

What makes the link convincing is not the correlation alone but the other evidence beside it: a **mechanism** (excess fat is known to make cells less responsive to insulin), the fact that the risk **rises steadily** as BMI rises rather than jumping about, and that **losing weight reduces** the risk — a change in the supposed cause producing a change in the effect.

So a top answer says: *the correlation is strong, and with a mechanism and the effect of weight loss it makes body mass a likely contributing cause — which is why obesity is called a **risk factor**: it raises the chance of type 2 without being the only cause, and correlation alone would not have shown even that.*

**Being exact about the two types.** Two phrasings lose marks:

- *Type 2 is caused by eating too much sugar* — sugar is not a direct cause. Obesity is a **risk factor** that raises the chance of type 2, and plenty of people with type 2 are not obese.
- *In type 2 the pancreas stops working* — it does not. The insulin is produced; the **cells stop responding** to it.

**Watch the two similar words.** Glyco**gen** is the **stored** substance. Gluca**gon** is the **hormone** that releases it. Writing the wrong one turns a correct explanation into a wrong one, and it happens constantly under time pressure.

**Watch the BMI arithmetic.** Square the height, use **metres**, and show height² on its own line. For an adult, mass ÷ height (not squared) is roughly 1.7 times the correct BMI, so the wrong answer can still look like a real BMI and a range check will not always catch it.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Cells need **glucose** for **respiration**, so blood glucose is held within narrow limits.
- It rises after a **meal** and falls during **exercise**, so it must be corrected in both directions.
- The **pancreas** produces both hormones.
- **Insulin** is released when glucose is **too high**. It moves glucose **into cells** and makes the **liver and muscles convert glucose into glycogen**. The level **falls**.
- **Glucagon** is released when glucose is **too low**. It makes the **liver convert glycogen into glucose**. The level **rises**.
- **Type 1 diabetes**: the pancreas does **not produce enough insulin**. Treated with **insulin injections**.
- **Type 2 diabetes**: the **cells stop responding** to insulin. Treated with a **carbohydrate-controlled diet** and **exercise**.
- **Obesity is a risk factor** for type 2: it raises the risk, but not everyone with type 2 is obese.
- $\text{BMI} = \dfrac{\text{mass (kg)}}{(\text{height (m)})^2}$ — square the height, and use metres.
- **Waist to hip ratio** = waist ÷ hip, both in the same unit. A higher ratio means more fat around the abdomen.
- A **correlation** between BMI and type 2 diabetes does **not by itself prove cause**; the mechanism and the effect of losing weight are what make the case.
- **Glycogen** is the store; **glucagon** is the hormone.

questions.prompt: Explain how the concentration of glucose in the blood is controlled after a large meal and then during a period of exercise, naming the hormones, the organ that produces them and the conversions involved.
questions.solution: After a large meal, carbohydrate is digested and glucose is absorbed into the blood, so the blood glucose concentration rises. The pancreas detects this rise and releases the hormone insulin into the blood. Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into body cells, and it also causes the liver and the muscles to convert glucose into glycogen, which is stored. Both of these remove glucose from the blood, so the concentration falls back towards normal. During exercise the muscles respire glucose rapidly, so the blood glucose concentration falls. The pancreas detects this fall and releases the hormone glucagon. Glucagon causes the liver to convert stored glycogen back into glucose, which is released into the blood, so the concentration rises back towards normal. In both cases the response opposes the change that triggered it, and as the level returns to normal the hormone stops being released, so the level does not overshoot. This is an example of negative feedback.

questions.modelAnswer:
**After a meal.** Carbohydrate is digested and glucose is absorbed, so the concentration **rises**.

- The **pancreas** detects the rise and releases **insulin**.
- Insulin causes glucose to move **from the blood into cells**.
- It also causes the **liver and muscles to convert glucose into glycogen** for storage.
- Both remove glucose from the blood, so the level **falls** back towards normal.

**During exercise.** The muscles respire glucose rapidly, so the concentration **falls**.

- The **pancreas** detects the fall and releases **glucagon**.
- Glucagon causes the **liver to convert glycogen back into glucose**, released into the blood.
- The level **rises** back towards normal.

**Why this is negative feedback.** Each response **opposes the change** that triggered it, and as the level returns to normal the hormone stops being released, so it does not overshoot.

The mark most often missed is insulin's **second** effect. Moving glucose into cells is only half of what it does; converting it to **glycogen** for storage is the other half.

questions.prompt: Compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Explain the cause of each, how each is controlled, and why the treatments differ.
questions.solution: In type 1 diabetes the pancreas does not produce enough insulin, and often produces none at all. It usually begins in childhood or early adulthood and is not caused by lifestyle. Because the problem is a shortage of insulin, it is controlled by injecting insulin, timed around meals and exercise, together with monitoring the diet and the blood glucose level. In type 2 diabetes the pancreas still produces insulin, but the body cells stop responding to it, a condition sometimes called insulin resistance. It usually develops later in life and obesity is a risk factor for it. Because the insulin is already present and is simply not being responded to, injecting more has a limited effect, so type 2 is controlled mainly through a carbohydrate controlled diet and increased exercise, which reduce the amount of glucose entering the blood and increase the amount used by the muscles. Drugs may also be used. The treatments differ because the two conditions fail at different points in the same control system: one is a failure to produce the hormone and the other is a failure to respond to it.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Type 1.** The **pancreas does not produce enough insulin**, often none at all. It usually begins in childhood or early adulthood and is **not** caused by lifestyle.

*Control*: **insulin injections**, timed around meals and exercise, with monitoring of diet and blood glucose.

**Type 2.** The pancreas **still produces insulin**, but the **body cells stop responding** to it. It usually develops later in life, and **obesity is a risk factor**.

*Control*: a **carbohydrate-controlled diet** and **more exercise**, which reduce the glucose entering the blood and increase the amount used by the muscles. Drugs may be added.

**Why the treatments differ.** The two conditions fail at **different points in the same control system**:

- Type 1 is a failure to **produce** the hormone, so supplying it works.
- Type 2 is a failure to **respond** to it, so supplying more has limited effect — the insulin is already there and being ignored.

That sentence is the one that turns a list of facts into a comparison, and it is where the last mark usually is.

questions.prompt:
A study followed a group of adults for ten years and recorded how many developed type 2 diabetes. The figures are illustrative.

| BMI category | Adults | Developed type 2 | Percentage |
|---|---|---|---|
| healthy weight | 2000 | 40 | 2% |
| overweight | 1500 | 75 | 5% |
| obese | 1000 | 120 | 12% |

Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
questions.solution: The percentage rises from 2% to 5% to 12% as BMI category rises, so **type 2 is more common at higher BMI** — a correlation. It does not prove cause on its own: a third factor such as diet or exercise could affect both. The other conclusions go beyond the data: 88% of obese adults did **not** develop it, 2% of healthy-weight adults did, and a rise from 2% to 12% is a clear link.

examTechnique.body:
Name the hormone, the gland and the organ it acts on separately, and state the conversion in the right direction.

Give both of insulin's effects: glucose into cells, and glucose stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles.

For the two types of diabetes, say where the failure is before saying how it is treated. The treatment follows from the cause.

In a BMI calculation, square the height first and keep it in metres. Show the squared value as a separate line, because it earns a method mark.

When a question gives data and asks what it shows, use the word correlation, and say what would be needed to establish cause.

Call obesity a **risk factor** for type 2 diabetes. If you argue that it is a cause, back the claim with the mechanism and the effect of losing weight, because the correlation alone does not show it.

Giving only one of insulin's two effects.
Saying the pancreas stops working in type 2 diabetes.
Saying type 1 is caused by diet.
Dividing by the height rather than by the height squared in a BMI calculation.
Saying a correlation proves that high BMI causes type 2 diabetes.
Saying glucagon is released when blood glucose is high.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats this as the same negative feedback as thyroxine, with two effectors instead of one, and says so. It gives both of insulin's effects without prompting. It separates the two types of diabetes by **where** the control system fails, and then derives the treatments from that rather than listing them. On the data question it uses the word correlation precisely, names what else would be needed for cause — a mechanism, and risk falling when weight is lost — and does not overstate what a single study shows. And its BMI working shows the squared height on its own line, which protects the method mark.
